title: Studying Abroad at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology
paragraphs: I did my clerkship at St. Olavs Hospital in Trondheim, the third largest city in Norway. In three months spent surrounded by rich nature and kind and independent Norwegians, I made many discoveries.

There are two points I felt were greatly different from Japan. The first is that healthcare is run efficiently under government leadership. In Norway only 5 million people live in a land the same size as Japan. The GP system has been adopted, and there are only four university hospitals. St. Olavs Hospital, where I did my clerkship, was one of them. The centre of the four university hospitals is Oslo University Hospital in the capital. Patients in each region who are judged to need advanced treatment are sent to this hospital by aircraft arranged by the state. Because charts are integrated nationwide, entries and test results from other hospitals can be viewed immediately. By thus concentrating specialised personnel and facilities in the university hospital of the capital and transmitting information smoothly, I felt that efficient medical care is delivered. The second difference is that there is almost no hierarchy and individuals are independent. During the three-month clerkship there was no occasion on which I felt a barrier of gender, age, occupation or nationality. More than 90% of both men and women take parental leave, and working until 16:00 is taken for granted. Also, there is no medical department system, and many doctors freely choose their department and hospital. I actually met a doctor who had moved through five departments. The relationship between doctor and patient is also flat, and I saw them putting their requests and questions to each other straight.

In February I trained in neurology, in March in pediatrics, and in April in thoracic surgery. In every department, conversations between doctors and with patients and chart entries are basically in Norwegian. For that reason, in the clerkships I mostly observed outpatient clinics, ward rounds and operations while receiving explanations in English as appropriate. I will introduce the specific content of the clerkship in each department and what left an impression.

February was neurology. At first it was not decided at all where I would do my clerkship or whom I would follow, and I had to speak up on my own every day, so I sometimes felt stressed. But gradually, as the number of doctors I knew increased, I was given many opportunities to work on procedures, and by doing neurological examinations and trying injections and lumbar punctures, it became a very fulfilling clerkship. Two things left an impression in neurology. The first was the large number of multiple sclerosis cases. I saw patients every day both in the outpatient clinic and on the ward and learned about the characteristics of the symptoms and treatment. The second was the diversity of treatments for migraine. In Norway it is said that one in four people has migraine, and research is thriving. I was surprised to witness symptoms improving dramatically with treatments I had never heard of in Japan, such as Botox and local anesthetic injections.

March was pediatrics. In the first week I trained in oncology, in the second week general, in the third week the NICU, and in the fourth week cardiology and emergency. Because the patients were children it was mainly observation, but sometimes I examined newborns, or took histories and did physical examinations on English-speaking patients. What left the greatest impression in pediatrics was how generous the support for patient children and families was. All the rooms were private rooms with a bed for the family, and a PS5 or Nintendo Switch was provided. In the NICU the private room was further divided into two rooms, with a bed for the newborn and a bed for the mother at the front, and at the back a bed for the father, with a toilet and shower fully equipped. There was also an initiative to ease the fear of the procedures children themselves would receive by having the child give injections and examine a mascot called Gusse. I thought the concept of warmly supporting the children with family and staff was lovely.

April was thoracic surgery. In thoracic surgery, students are prohibited from entering the operative field, so the clerkship was basically observing surgery. What left an impression was how the doctors work. Unlike Japan, thoracic surgeons operate on both the heart and the lungs. For that reason, my impression was that the minimum necessary operations are chosen, for example that a heart-lung machine is always used for coronary artery bypass and that the da Vinci had only just been introduced for lung cancer surgery. Also, except for emergencies, operations were planned only Monday to Thursday so as to finish by 16:00, and all the doctors went home on time. All difficult cases are sent to Oslo, and I was impressed by the efficient way of working that is possible precisely because medical resources are concentrated.

Locally I lived in a student dormitory. While living with two people of different roots and faculties, I could talk a lot about cultural differences and the future, which broadened my horizons. In my free time, I ate and went out with a student who had come to Nagoya last year. Experiencing Norwegian culture such as home cooking and Easter together with a local student was a different kind of enjoyment from travelling. On days off I also travelled around Europe with classmates. Even when tired from the clerkship, speaking in Japanese reset my feelings, and the following week I was able to take on the clerkship positively again.

When writing this report, looking back over the notes I had saved up locally, I realised that I had been given far more experiences than fit on several sheets of A4. While receiving new stimulation every day, I think I was able to take an objective look at myself, who will become a doctor in Japan. I would like to express my thanks to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office who made efforts for this program, and to everyone who looked after me locally.
